title: Tested in the Wilderness, Rejected at Home
summary: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is tested by the devil for forty days in the wilderness and answers each temptation from Deuteronomy. Back in Galilee he reads Isaiah 61 in the Nazareth synagogue and announces that it is fulfilled today, but his hometown turns on him when he recalls God's mercy to foreigners. In Capernaum he drives out demons, heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, and then moves on to preach the kingdom of God in other towns.
story: At the Jordan the Father named Jesus his beloved Son, and the genealogy traced him back to Adam, the son of God. Now that sonship is tested. Where Adam fell in a garden and Israel grumbled forty years in the wilderness, Jesus holds firm in the wilderness for forty days. Then Luke opens the public ministry with a scene he treats as a program for everything that follows: the sermon in Nazareth. Good news for the poor, release for captives, sight for the blind, a welcome that reaches beyond Israel, and rejection by his own people are all here in miniature. The rest of the chapter shows the announcement becoming deed in Capernaum.
historical:
Galilee, the northern region where Jesus grew up and did most of his work, was ruled by Herod Antipas as tetrarch under Rome. It was largely Jewish in the first century, farmed and fished, with villages clustered around the Sea of Galilee. Nazareth was a small hill village; excavations suggest a modest agricultural settlement of perhaps a few hundred people, a few miles from Sepphoris, which Antipas rebuilt as a regional city. Capernaum sat on the northwest shore of the lake, near the border with Philip's territory, and became Jesus' base. The limestone synagogue visible there today dates from centuries later, but it stands over earlier basalt foundations that some archaeologists connect with the synagogue of Jesus' time.

Mark 6:1-6 and Matthew 13:53-58 also tell of Jesus' rejection at Nazareth, but place it later in his ministry and give no synagogue reading. Luke brings the scene to the front, probably deliberately, because it sets out his whole understanding of Jesus' mission. The verse 23 reference to what Jesus had already done in Capernaum shows that Luke knows the visit did not come first.
cultural:
A synagogue (from a Greek word for a gathering) was a local assembly and meeting place for prayer, the reading of Scripture, and teaching. On the Sabbath a portion from the Law of Moses was read, then a reading from the Prophets, and a qualified man might be invited to comment. Scripture was kept on scrolls, rolled on rods, and handed out by an attendant. Readers stood to read in honor of the text and sat down to teach, which is why every eye is on Jesus when he sits.

The words Jesus reads come from Isaiah 61:1-2, with a phrase from Isaiah 58:6 (“to release the oppressed”) woven in. Isaiah's language of liberty and a year of favor draws on the Jubilee of Leviticus 25, the fiftieth year when debts were cancelled, slaves freed, and land returned to its families. Jesus stops mid-sentence, before Isaiah's next line about the day of vengeance. His examples of Elijah and Elisha would have stung: in the stories of 1 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 5, God's help went to a widow in Sidon, a Gentile land, and to Naaman, the commander of a hostile Syrian army. The proverb “Physician, heal yourself” was a common saying demanding that someone prove himself at home.
literary: The temptation has three rounds, each with the devil's offer and Jesus' answer from Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:13, 6:16), the book in which Moses reminds Israel of its own testing in the wilderness. In the third round the devil quotes Scripture too (Psalm 91:11-12), showing that the Bible can be quoted to wrong ends. Matthew 4:1-11 has the same three tests but ends on the mountain; Luke ends in Jerusalem at the temple, the city toward which his whole Gospel moves. The Nazareth scene is built with slow care: standing, receiving, unrolling, finding, reading, rolling up, returning, sitting, and then the single sentence “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.” The mood swings from admiration to fury in a few verses. The Capernaum episodes (31-44) follow Mark 1:21-39 closely.

outline.t: Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Spirit
The reading from Isaiah in Nazareth
Elijah, Elisha, and the hometown's rejection
Authority over an unclean spirit in Capernaum
Sent to preach the kingdom in other towns

doctrines.note: Luke stresses the Spirit at every turn: Jesus is full of the Spirit, led by the Spirit, returns in the power of the Spirit, and reads that the Spirit of the Lord is on him. His ministry is the Spirit's work, the same Spirit he will later give his followers.
To be anointed is what the title Messiah (Hebrew) or Christ (Greek) means. Jesus claims Isaiah's anointed messenger as himself, and the demons in verse 41 know him as the Christ.

The Nazareth sermon points outward: good news to the poor and the captive, and God's mercy reaching Sidon and Syria. Verse 43 adds that Jesus was sent to other towns as well. The mission is not held for one place or one people.

words.note: Chrio, to anoint. In Israel kings, priests, and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil to mark them for God's service. From this verb comes christos, the anointed one. Jesus is anointed not with oil but with the Spirit, as Acts 10:38 also says.

Aphesis, release or forgiveness. The same word Luke uses for the forgiveness of sins (as in 3:3) here translates liberty for captives and release for the oppressed. In the Greek Old Testament it names the Jubilee release. Luke lets the two senses sit together: Jesus brings release from every kind of bondage.

Semeron, today. A small word with great weight in Luke: today a Savior is born (2:11), today this Scripture is fulfilled (4:21), today salvation has come to this house (19:9), today you will be with me in Paradise (23:43). God's long promises arrive in the present tense.

Peirazo, to test or tempt. The word covers both a trial meant to prove someone and an enticement to do wrong. The devil tempts; God allows the testing, and Jesus proves faithful where Israel had failed.

christ: Every temptation aims at the title just given at the baptism, “If You are the Son of God”, and invites Jesus to prove it by using his power for himself, seizing the world's kingdoms without the cross, or forcing God's hand. He refuses each time, choosing trust and obedience as a true Israelite and true son. At Nazareth he claims to be the one Isaiah spoke of, anointed by the Spirit to bring good news to the poor. The fulfillment is not a program he will one day start; it happens as he speaks. The rejection that follows, ending at the edge of a cliff, foreshadows the cross, and his walking away through the crowd shows that his life will be taken only when he gives it.

hard.q: Why did the people of Nazareth turn so quickly from admiration to trying to kill Jesus?
hard.a: The difficulty is real: they speak well of him in verse 22 and try to throw him off a cliff by verse 29. Several things help. Their question, “Isn’t this the son of Joseph?”, can be read either as pleased surprise or as the start of doubt that a local carpenter's son could make such claims. Jesus anticipates that they want him to perform miracles for his own town, as he had in Capernaum. His answer, drawn from their own Scriptures, is that God's prophets had been sent to outsiders when Israel would not receive them. To a village living under foreign rule and hoping for God's favor on Israel, the suggestion that the promised release might pass them by and reach Gentiles felt like an insult. Some interpreters stress the offense of his claim to fulfill Isaiah; others stress the offense of the widening of grace. Luke likely intends both, and he will show the same pattern again in Acts, where the gospel is refused by many in Israel and received by Gentiles.

questions: Jesus answers the devil with Scripture, and the devil quotes Scripture too. What separates a faithful use of the Bible from a manipulative one?
In Isaiah's list, the poor, the captives, the blind, and the oppressed receive good news. Who are those people in your community, and what would good news mean to them?
The people of Nazareth were offended that God's mercy reached outsiders. Where might you resent God being generous to someone you would rather he passed over?
